title: Evolutionary Particle Filter Data Assimilation With a Complex Process‐Based Hydrologic Model for Enhancing Streamflow Prediction
content:
Abstract

Accurate streamflow prediction remains fundamental for water resources management, flood forecasting applications, and climate adaptation strategies. Physics-based hydrological models provide process understanding and spatial transferability, yet uncertainties in model structure, initial conditions, parameter values, and meteorological inputs limit prediction reliability. Data assimilation is a widely used strategy for improving model predictions by constraining model states with observational information. This research develops and evaluates a data assimilation approach, integrating the Evolutionary Ensemble Particle Filter with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (EPFM) with the Structure for Unifying Multiple Modeling Alternatives (SUMMA) process-based hydrological modeling system across 66 northeastern United States watersheds. This ensemble approach manages computational complexities of particle communication during evolutionary operations, implementing global synchronization protocols at each timestep with coordinated memory management among ensemble members. The system executes data assimilation, updating critical state variables including soil moisture, snow water equivalent, and canopy storage through the assimilation of daily streamflow observations within hourly model execution cycles. Evaluation results show substantial performance enhancements, with 94% of the watersheds demonstrating improved streamflow simulations in terms of Coefficient of determination. The Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency and Kling–Gupta Efficiency improved in 95.5% and 86.4% of the watersheds, respectively. The research demonstrates that the EPFM method is a viable strategy to improve the accuracy of streamflow simulation in a complex process-based hydrological model, while also providing critical understanding of parameter-state variable relationships and temporal resolution effects, offering potential benefits for hydrologic process model applications, including watershed studies, monitoring and forecasting.
